texts.0: SP, due to a delayed power reduction after each level-off call, did not stabilize the assigned altitude during vectoring and allowed the altitude deviation until on final to exceed 300 ft. The excursion continued through the controller's altitude correction and the IP intervened to arrest the descent before the next vector. SP did not re-establish the assigned altitude before intercepting the final approach course.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete scan of the altimeter while working the assigned vector headings, let the altitude deviation until on final reach 300 ft. SP corrected only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP and the return to the assigned altitude was slow. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slow trim adjustment after gear extension, let the assigned altitude drift between 150 ft and 300 ft during vectoring. SP detected the trend on the altimeter and returned to the assigned altitude before the controller called the deviation. No prompting and no intervention were needed.
texts.3: SP maintained every assigned altitude during vectoring within 150 ft. Power and trim were adjusted promptly at each level-off and the aircraft was stable in altitude before the next controller instruction. The altimeter was cross-checked regularly throughout the pattern.
texts.4: SP held every assigned altitude until on final with deviations that were barely perceptible on the altimeter. Level-offs were anticipated and power was set so that no follow-up correction was needed. Altitude control remained precise through configuration changes and vectoring turns.
texts.marginal: SP kept the altitude deviation until on final inside the required standards, but corrections tended to start late and were applied in large steps rather than small ones. The deviations grew mainly during vectoring turns combined with configuration changes. SP is expected to anticipate level-offs earlier and to hold the assigned altitude with smaller, smoother corrections.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the assigned altitude during vectoring with the deviation settling at the 300 ft limit, due to an incomplete scan of the altimeter while working the assigned vector headings. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to include the altimeter in the scan through every vector heading change so the deviation does not reach the 300 ft limit.
texts_at.2: SP maintained the assigned altitude during vectoring with the deviation settling at about 200 ft, due to a slow trim adjustment after gear extension. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to trim for the new configuration the moment gear is selected rather than after the deviation shows.
texts_at.3: SP maintained every assigned altitude during vectoring within 150 ft, due to one level-off correction applied a few seconds after the level-off call rather than at it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to act on the level-off call at the instant it is received rather than a moment later.

texts_above.2: SP detected the altitude trend on the altimeter after the deviation drifted to about 200 ft and returned to the assigned altitude before the controller called the deviation, without prompting or intervention. Trimming for the new configuration the moment gear is selected would keep that drift smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.3: SP maintained every assigned altitude during vectoring within 150 ft, with power and trim adjusted promptly at each level-off and the aircraft stable before the next controller instruction. The only refinement available is to act on the level-off call at the instant it is received rather than a moment later. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.4: SP held every assigned altitude until on final with deviations that were barely perceptible on the altimeter, with level-offs anticipated and power set so no follow-up correction was needed. There is little left to refine; every level-off is already anticipated rather than corrected into. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude discipline on the vectors.

texts.0: SP, due to uncoordinated and over-controlled turns onto the assigned vectors, exceeded 10 deg of deviation from the headings issued by the GCA controller. SP overshot successive vectors and the resulting track took the aircraft off the final approach course, so the IP intervened to re-intercept. Heading control was not re-established by SP without help.
texts.1: SP, due to rolling out without cross-checking the heading indicator, allowed heading deviations of about 10 deg from the assigned vectors. SP returned to the assigned heading only after verbal prompting and applied the corrections with delay. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly high roll rate on the turns to final, rolled out with heading deviations between 5 deg and 10 deg from the assigned vectors. SP recognized the error on the heading indicator and corrected back promptly with small bank inputs. No prompting and no IP intervention were needed.
texts.3: SP flew every heading issued by the GCA controller within 5 deg. Turns were started immediately on receipt, bank was appropriate and roll-out was anticipated so that the assigned heading was captured without overshoot. The heading was then held steady until the next instruction.
texts.4: SP flew the assigned vectors with heading deviations that were hardly readable on the indicator. Each turn was rolled out exactly on the ordered heading and the aircraft was kept there without wandering. Drift corrections on final were small and continuous.
texts.marginal: SP held the assigned headings within the standards, but tended to overshoot slightly on each turn and then chase the heading back with repeated small corrections. This was most evident on the turn to the final approach course. SP is expected to anticipate roll-out and settle on the assigned heading with a single correction.

texts_at.1: SP flew the assigned vectors with heading deviation settling at about 10 deg, due to rolling out without cross-checking the heading indicator on one turn. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to cross-check the heading indicator on every roll-out, not only when a deviation is suspected.
texts_at.2: SP flew the assigned vectors with heading deviation settling between 5 deg and 10 deg, due to a slightly high roll rate on the turn to final. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to match the roll rate to the heading change required rather than using the same rate for every turn.
texts_at.3: SP flew every heading issued by the GCA controller within 5 deg, due to one roll-out anticipated a fraction late before the assigned heading was captured. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to anticipate the roll-out on every turn as consistently as on the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the heading error between 5 deg and 10 deg on the heading indicator and corrected back promptly with small bank inputs, without prompting or intervention. Matching the roll rate to the heading change required, rather than using the same rate for every turn, would keep the error smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound heading discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.3: SP flew every heading issued by the GCA controller within 5 deg, with turns started immediately on receipt and roll-out anticipated so the assigned heading was captured without overshoot. The only refinement available is to anticipate the very first roll-out as consistently as the later ones. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed heading discipline on the vectors.
texts_above.4: SP flew the assigned vectors with heading deviations that were hardly readable on the indicator, with each turn rolled out exactly on the ordered heading and drift corrections on final kept small and continuous. There is little left to refine; every roll-out is already exact rather than corrected into. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional heading discipline on the vectors.

texts.0: SP, due to power settings not being adjusted for the configuration changes, exceeded the airspeed limits of the approach, going more than 20 kt fast during vectoring and more than 10 kt slow later on final. The excursions were not detected in time and the IP intervened with the throttle to restore the approach speed. Approach speed was never stabilized by SP.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction when gear and flaps were selected, let the airspeed reach 20 kt above the target and later 10 kt below it. SP corrected only after verbal prompting and the airspeed returned to target slowly. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to slightly coarse throttle handling during the configuration change, allowed airspeed excursions between 10 kt and 20 kt fast and between 5 kt and 10 kt slow. SP saw the trend on the airspeed indicator and set the correct power to recapture the target speed without prompting. Airspeed was stable well before the final descent.
texts.3: SP flew the approach within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow of the target airspeed at all times. Power was set correctly for each configuration change and the airspeed was stable on final. Airspeed was cross-checked regularly together with attitude and altitude.
texts.4: SP held the target airspeed with negligible deviations throughout vectoring and the final approach. Configuration changes produced no noticeable speed excursion because power was set in anticipation. Airspeed remained on target all the way to the transition to landing.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed inside the required standards, but it drifted repeatedly toward the fast side after each configuration change and needed several throttle corrections to settle. Speed stability was achieved only late on final. SP is expected to anticipate the power change with the configuration and to hold the target airspeed with fewer and smaller adjustments.

texts_at.1: SP held the target airspeed with the deviation settling at about 20 kt fast during vectoring, due to a late power reduction when gear and flaps were selected. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to reduce power at the moment gear and flaps are selected rather than a beat afterward.
texts_at.2: SP held the target airspeed with the deviation settling between 10 kt and 20 kt fast, due to slightly coarse throttle handling during the configuration change. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make the throttle change in smaller, more deliberate steps at the configuration change.
texts_at.3: SP flew the approach within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow of the target airspeed at all times, due to one power correction made a beat after the airspeed indicator had already started to move. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the power change with the configuration itself rather than reacting to the indicator.

texts_above.2: SP saw the trend on the airspeed indicator after the deviation moved between 10 kt and 20 kt fast and set the correct power to recapture the target speed without prompting, with airspeed stable well before the final descent. Making the throttle change in smaller, more deliberate steps at the configuration change would keep the excursion smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid power management on the approach.
texts_above.3: SP flew the approach within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow of the target airspeed at all times, with power set correctly for each configuration change and airspeed cross-checked regularly with attitude and altitude. The only refinement available is to anticipate the very first power change with the configuration itself. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed power management on the approach.
texts_above.4: SP held the target airspeed with negligible deviations throughout vectoring and the final approach, with configuration changes producing no noticeable speed excursion because power was set in anticipation. There is little left to refine; every power change is already anticipated rather than reacted to. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding power management on the approach.

texts.0: SP, due to a pitch and power combination not matched to the controller's glide path calls, went more than 300 ft above and later more than 150 ft below the glide path. SP did not respond correctly to the repeated below glide path calls and the IP intervened to arrest the sink rate. The approach as flown could not have been continued to minima.
texts.1: SP, due to correcting with pitch alone instead of a coordinated pitch and power input, reached about 300 ft above and about 150 ft below the glide path. SP regained the glide path only after verbal prompting and the corrections lagged the controller's calls. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to slightly late responses to the controller's rate of descent calls, drifted from slightly above the glide path toward the 300 ft high band and later toward the 150 ft low band. SP recognized the trend from the sequence of controller calls and re-established the glide path in good time with a coordinated pitch and power correction. No prompting and no intervention were needed.
texts.3: SP tracked the glide path throughout the PAR final, remaining only slightly above or slightly below it. Corrections were made with small coordinated pitch and power changes as each controller call was received. Rate of descent was kept steady and appropriate to the groundspeed.
texts.4: SP flew the PAR final on the glide path with deviations the controller reported as negligible. Each on glide path call was maintained by anticipating rate of descent changes rather than by reacting to them. The descent rate remained smooth and constant from glide path intercept to minima.
texts.marginal: SP stayed within the glide path standards but tended to sit consistently on the high side and then correct with an increased rate of descent. The high-then-steep pattern repeated over the second half of the final. SP is expected to intercept the glide path more precisely and to hold it with smaller rate of descent changes.

texts_at.1: SP tracked the PAR glide path with a pitch and power correction settling at about 300 ft above and about 150 ft below on separate occasions, due to correcting with pitch alone instead of a coordinated pitch and power input. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to correct every glide-path deviation with pitch and power together rather than pitch alone.
texts_at.2: SP tracked the PAR glide path with the vertical speed exceeding about 400 feet per minute from the required rate before it was recognized, due to slightly late responses to the controller's rate of descent calls. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to act on each rate of descent call as it is received rather than after a short delay.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the glide path throughout the PAR final, remaining only slightly above or slightly below it, due to one rate of descent change that lagged the controller's call by a beat before the coordinated correction was applied. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to match the pitch and power correction to the call at the moment it is received.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the trend from the sequence of controller calls and re-established the glide path in good time with a coordinated pitch and power correction, without prompting or intervention, after the vertical speed had exceeded about 400 feet per minute from the required rate. Acting on each rate of descent call as it is received, rather than after a short delay, would keep that swing smaller. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to steady glide-path tracking.
texts_above.3: SP tracked the glide path throughout the PAR final, remaining only slightly above or slightly below it, with corrections made in small coordinated pitch and power changes as each controller call was received. The only refinement available is to match the correction to the call at the moment it is received rather than a beat later. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate glide-path tracking.
texts_above.4: SP flew the PAR final on the glide path with deviations the controller reported as negligible, anticipating rate of descent changes rather than reacting to them and holding the descent rate smooth and constant from intercept to minima. There is little left to refine; every rate change is already anticipated rather than answered. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary glide-path tracking.

texts.0: SP, due to failing to build a clear picture from the controller's calls, applied corrections in the wrong sense, turning away from the ordered heading correction and increasing the rate of descent after an above glide path call. Compliance with ATC instructions was not achieved and the aircraft diverged from the final approach course. The IP intervened to correct the aircraft and re-establish the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to processing each controller instruction only after the following one had been transmitted, responded to the GCA corrections late throughout the final. Corrections were applied only after verbal prompting by the IP and several instructions had to be repeated by the controller. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly slow interpretation of the controller's calls, responded to the heading and glide path corrections with a noticeable delay in the first part of the final. SP recognized the lag, tightened the response and was matching each call promptly by mid final. No prompting and no intervention were needed.
texts.3: SP complied with every GCA instruction immediately and in the correct sense. Each heading and glide path correction was applied with a magnitude appropriate to the reported deviation and the controller did not have to repeat any call. Instructions for gear, checks and minima were acknowledged and executed on time.
texts.4: SP responded to the controller's instructions with immediate and precisely sized corrections, so that most calls returned to on course and on glide path. The approach required only minimal further guidance from the controller. Every instruction was acknowledged and executed without hesitation.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the controller's instructions within standards, but the corrections were often larger than the reported deviation required and then had to be taken out again. This produced a slight oscillation about course and glide path. SP is expected to size each correction to the deviation called and to hold it rather than over-correct.

texts_at.1: SP responded to the GCA corrections with one heading correction applied only after a second controller call, due to processing each instruction only after the following one had already been transmitted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to action each controller call before the next one is transmitted rather than holding two in memory at once.
texts_at.2: SP responded to the heading and glide path corrections with a short delay in the first part of the final, due to a slightly slow interpretation of the controller's calls. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to shorten the interval between hearing the call and applying the correction from the very first instruction.
texts_at.3: SP complied with every GCA instruction immediately and in the correct sense, with corrections sized to the reported deviation, due to one correction that was a fraction late while the previous one was still being trimmed out. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete each correction before the next call is due rather than carrying it into the following instruction.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the lag in responding to the controller's calls, tightened the response and was matching each call promptly by mid final, without prompting or intervention. Shortening the interval between hearing the call and applying the correction from the very first instruction would remove that lag entirely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable response discipline on the GCA.
texts_above.3: SP complied with every GCA instruction immediately and in the correct sense, with each heading and glide path correction sized to the reported deviation and no call repeated by the controller. The only refinement available is to complete each correction before the next call is due rather than carrying it forward. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good response discipline on the GCA.
texts_above.4: SP responded to the controller's instructions with immediate and precisely sized corrections, so most calls returned to on course and on glide path with only minimal further guidance needed. There is little left to refine; every instruction is already acknowledged and executed without hesitation. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior response discipline on the GCA.

error_modes.label: Radio discipline and readbacks with GCA

texts.0: SP, due to non-standard phraseology on the approach frequency, transmitted acknowledgements that identified neither the aircraft nor the instruction and did not read back the assigned altitudes and headings. One instruction was consequently misunderstood and the IP had to take the radios to clarify with the controller. Compliance with ATC instructions was not maintained.
texts.1: SP, due to using non-standard wording instead of the prescribed calls, made readbacks that were incomplete and had to be corrected by the controller. SP applied the correct phraseology only after verbal prompting by the IP. Radio work remained slow, but no intervention on the controls was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to occasional non-standard wording under the higher radio workload of the PAR, made two readbacks that omitted part of the instruction. SP noticed the omission and re-transmitted the complete readback before the controller queried it. Radio discipline was correct for the remainder of the approach.
texts.3: SP used standard phraseology on the GCA frequency throughout the approach. Every clearance, heading and altitude was read back correctly and acknowledgements were concise and timely. SP maintained the required transmissions during the no-transmission segment of the PAR final.
texts.4: SP handled the GCA frequency with precise standard phraseology and no wasted transmissions. Readbacks were complete and immediate and never interfered with aircraft control. Radio work required no correction from either the controller or the IP.
texts.marginal: SP kept radio work within standards, but phraseology drifted toward informal wording as the workload increased on final and readbacks became abbreviated. Aircraft control also degraded slightly while transmitting. SP is expected to keep standard phraseology under load and to separate radio work from control inputs.

texts_at.1: SP handled the GCA frequency with readbacks that were correct but needed the controller to wait once for a complete transmission, due to non-standard phraseology under the higher radio workload of the approach. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to use the prescribed phraseology even as the radio workload increases on final.
texts_at.2: SP handled the GCA frequency with two readbacks that omitted part of the instruction before the omission was caught, due to occasional non-standard wording under the higher radio workload of the PAR. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check each readback against the instruction received before transmitting it.
texts_at.3: SP used standard phraseology on the GCA frequency throughout the approach, with clearances read back correctly and acknowledgements concise and timely, due to one transmission made a beat before the required maintenance of the no-transmission segment. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the no-transmission segment boundaries before every transmission on the approach.

texts_above.2: SP noticed the incomplete readback and re-transmitted the complete version before the controller queried it, correcting the pattern without IP input for the remainder of the approach. Checking each readback against the instruction received, before transmitting it, would prevent the omission from occurring at all. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured radio discipline on the GCA.
texts_above.3: SP used standard phraseology on the GCA frequency throughout the approach, with every clearance, heading and altitude read back correctly and the required transmissions maintained during the no-transmission segment of the PAR final. The only refinement available is to confirm the segment boundaries before every transmission rather than most of them. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise radio discipline on the GCA.
texts_above.4: SP handled the GCA frequency with precise standard phraseology and no wasted transmissions, with readbacks complete and immediate and never interfering with aircraft control. There is little left to refine; radio work never competes with the flying task. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate radio discipline on the GCA.

error_modes.label: Approach sequence, configuration and checks
error_modes.source: general:c (executes the approach according to standardized procedures without mistakes and IP intervention)

texts.0: SP, due to an unrehearsed approach sequence, did not complete the before-landing checks at the correct points and selected gear and landing flaps out of order and late on final. The approach was not executed according to the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the flight manual, and the IP intervened to complete the configuration. Several procedural steps were omitted entirely.
texts.1: SP, due to weak recall of the GCA procedure sequence, ran the descent and before-landing checks out of the prescribed order and completed them late. The missing items were caught only after verbal prompting by the IP. No IP action on the controls was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly rushed set-up after the vector to final, started the before-landing check later than briefed. SP identified the delay and completed the check in the correct sequence in time for glide path intercept. The rest of the procedure followed the standardized sequence without prompting.
texts.3: SP executed the GCA procedure in the correct sequence, with configuration changes and checks completed at the standard points. The approach was flown in accordance with the flight manual, the MAIP and local area procedures without mistakes and without IP intervention. The aircraft was configured and stabilized before glide path intercept.
texts.4: SP executed the whole PAR procedure fluently and in the exact prescribed sequence, with every check completed early enough to leave full capacity for flying the approach. Configuration changes were timed so that the aircraft was fully stabilized well before the final descent. No item required prompting at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP followed the standardized sequence within standards, but each check was completed close to the last acceptable point and left little margin before glide path intercept. The same pattern was repeated on both approaches. SP is expected to start the descent and before-landing checks earlier so that the aircraft is configured and stabilized ahead of final.

texts_at.1: SP completed the approach sequence with the before-landing check started later than briefed, due to weak recall of the GCA procedure sequence under the workload of the descent. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to review the procedure sequence before the descent so recall does not depend on the workload at the time.
texts_at.2: SP completed the approach sequence with the before-landing check started a few seconds later than briefed, due to a slightly rushed set-up after the vector to final. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to begin the set-up on receipt of the vector to final rather than after it is complete.
texts_at.3: SP executed the GCA procedure in the correct sequence with configuration changes and checks completed at the standard points, due to one check that was started at the latest acceptable point rather than with margin ahead of it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to give every check the same margin as the others rather than the latest acceptable point.

texts_above.2: SP identified the delay in the before-landing check and completed it in the correct sequence in time for glide path intercept, without prompting or intervention, with the rest of the procedure following the standardized sequence. Beginning the set-up on receipt of the vector to final, rather than after it, would remove that delay. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent procedural discipline on the approach.
texts_above.3: SP executed the GCA procedure in the correct sequence, with configuration changes and checks completed at the standard points and the aircraft configured and stabilized before glide path intercept. The only refinement available is to give every check the same margin as the others rather than the latest acceptable point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined procedural execution on the approach.
texts_above.4: SP executed the whole PAR procedure fluently and in the exact prescribed sequence, with every check completed early enough to leave full capacity for flying the approach and the aircraft stabilized well before the final descent. There is little left to refine; the procedure is already ahead of the aircraft rather than reacting to it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to faultless procedural execution on the approach.

error_modes.label: Restrictions, minima and the decision at DH
error_modes.source: general:b (routing and altitude restrictions per MAIP and Instrument Approach Manuals) | general:c

texts.0: SP, due to continuation bias after the controller reported the aircraft slightly below glide path near minima, continued the descent past the published minimum without the required visual references. The published altitude restrictions of the MAIP and the approach manual were violated and the IP intervened to initiate the missed approach. The decision point was passed without any decision being made.
texts.1: SP, due to continuation bias on an approach that had been flown low on the glide path, held the descent at the published minimum although the criteria for continuing were not satisfied. SP initiated the missed approach only after being told verbally to do so and the initiation was late. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a late assessment of the approach against the published minima, allowed the aircraft to reach the minimum descent point before deciding. SP then recognized that the criteria were not met and executed the missed approach correctly without prompting. No routing or altitude restriction was violated.
texts.3: SP respected every routing and altitude restriction published in the MAIP and the instrument approach manual. The decision at minima was taken at the correct point and the resulting action, continuation to land or missed approach, was executed according to the published procedure. No restriction was approached without awareness of it.
texts.4: SP flew the approach with the published routing and altitude restrictions anticipated well in advance and briefed before each segment. The decision at minima was taken exactly at the published point and stated clearly, and the missed approach was flown precisely as published. The approach was never allowed to develop toward a restriction.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the published restrictions and minima, but assessed the approach only at the last moment instead of progressively during the final. This left minimal time to prepare the missed approach. SP is expected to evaluate the approach continuously against the published criteria and to pre-commit to the action at minima.

texts_at.1: SP respected the routing and altitude restrictions and decided at minima with the assessment completed only after reaching the minimum descent point, due to a late assessment of the approach against the published minima. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to begin the assessment earlier on the final so the decision is ready at the minimum descent point.
texts_at.2: SP respected every restriction and minimum with the assessment completed at the minimum descent point rather than slightly ahead of it, due to attention held on the glide path corrections through the final segment. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the assessment a few seconds ahead of the minimum descent point rather than exactly at it.
texts_at.3: SP respected every routing and altitude restriction published in the MAIP and the instrument approach manual, with the decision at minima taken at the correct point, due to the assessment being finished right at the point itself rather than slightly ahead of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the assessment a moment earlier so the decision never depends on reaching the point first.

texts_above.2: SP recognized that the criteria for continuing were not met and executed the missed approach correctly on its own initiative, with no routing or altitude restriction violated. Completing the assessment a few seconds ahead of the minimum descent point, rather than exactly at it, would let the decision be made with margin. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good judgement at minima.
texts_above.3: SP respected every routing and altitude restriction published in the MAIP and the instrument approach manual, with the decision at minima taken at the correct point and the resulting action executed according to the published procedure. The only refinement available is to complete the assessment a fraction earlier so no part of the decision trails the point itself. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good judgement at minima.
texts_above.4: SP flew the approach with the published routing and altitude restrictions anticipated well in advance and briefed before each segment, with the decision at minima taken exactly at the published point and stated clearly. There is little left to refine; the decision is already committed before the point is reached. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent judgement at minima.

error_modes.label: Instrument cross-check under PAR radio load
error_modes.source: general:c (executes the final approach without mistakes and IP intervention)

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while concentrating on the controller's continuous transmissions, stopped monitoring attitude and airspeed on the final. Several parameters degraded at the same time and the aircraft reached a state the IP had to correct. The approach was not flown by reference to the primary flight instruments as required.
texts.1: SP, due to a cross-check that fixated on the attitude indicator and left airspeed and altitude unmonitored, allowed parameters to reach the limits of the approach standards before noticing them. SP resumed a full scan only after verbal prompting by the IP. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that slowed while the controller's calls were being processed, let attitude and airspeed drift beyond the precise band before detection. SP restored a regular scan of the primary flight instruments and recovered the parameters in good time. No prompting and no intervention were needed.
texts.3: SP maintained a regular instrument cross-check throughout the PAR, covering attitude, airspeed, altitude and heading while working the controller's instructions. Deviations were detected as trends and corrected before they became significant. Aircraft state was monitored continuously down to minima.
texts.4: SP maintained a fast and complete instrument cross-check under the continuous radio load of the PAR final, so that no parameter was left unmonitored at any time. Deviations were anticipated from the rate of change of the instruments rather than from their values. Aircraft state was known at every point of the approach.
texts.marginal: SP kept a cross-check adequate to hold the standards, but it narrowed noticeably each time the controller transmitted, with altitude and airspeed checked less often than attitude. Deviations were detected as values rather than as trends. SP is expected to keep the scan rate constant under radio load and to detect trends earlier.

texts_at.1: SP maintained the instrument cross-check with attitude and airspeed reaching the limits of the approach standards before the deviation was noticed, due to a cross-check that fixated on the attitude indicator while the controller was transmitting.
